explanations.answer: He presses on to take hold of it
explanations.explanation: Paul says he presses on to take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of him. He's not claiming to be finished, and he's not sitting still either. Friend, that's a man in motion. I'll take a teacher who admits he's still on the road over one who pretends he's already home.

explanations.answer: He waits for it to come to him
explanations.explanation: Paul never says he waits. He says he presses on, and that's the opposite of parking yourself by the door. I once waited for a batch to bake itself, friend. Nobody had turned the oven on, and the dough just sat there looking at me.

explanations.answer: He rests on what he has done
explanations.explanation: Paul says the reverse. He says he hasn't already obtained all this and hasn't already been made perfect, so resting isn't what he does. What he does is press on. A cooling rack is great, but Paul still has dough on the counter.

Paul says, "Forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead…" (Philippians 3:13). Notice he doesn't list what's behind, so I won't either. His eyes are pointed forward, and he's straining toward it. That's a man who is going somewhere.
Close, because it's a direction word. But Paul says what is behind, not what is around him. The rest of the sentence points the other way, toward what is ahead. Forward is where he's straining.

Paul never mentions an audience in this verse. He says he's forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead. Good news, friend: nobody's clipboard is in this sentence. It's just Paul and the road in front of him.

Paul presses on toward the goal to win the prize of God's heavenly calling in Christ Jesus. A goal and a prize go together, and he has both in view. He's not wandering, friend. He knows exactly where he's headed.

Approval is what I'd have guessed too, friend. I'm always checking whether the dough likes me. But Paul says he presses on toward the goal to win the prize of God's heavenly calling in Christ Jesus. The verse puts a prize at the finish line, so prize is the word.

Rest sounds lovely, I won't lie. But Paul's whole sentence is about pressing on and straining, and the word he lands on is prize. He says it's the prize of God's heavenly calling in Christ Jesus. Rest just isn't the word in this verse.

Paul says, "And if you think differently about some issue, God will reveal this to you as well." Look who does the revealing: God. Paul isn't promising to win every debate himself. I find that a relief, friend.

The text says the opposite of False. Paul says, "And if you think differently about some issue, God will reveal this to you as well." So the statement is true, and God is the one who reveals it. Paul doesn't say he'll do it himself.

explanations.answer: Live up to what we have already attained
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "Nevertheless, we must live up to what we have already attained." Even where people think differently, there's something already in hand to live by. So you don't have to wait for every question to be settled. You can walk in what you've already got.

explanations.answer: Keep quiet until everyone finally agrees
explanations.explanation: Paul says nothing about staying quiet. He says we must live up to what we have already attained. Waiting for total agreement would take longer than a Monday morning meeting, friend. Paul keeps people moving.

explanations.answer: Stop and wait until more is revealed
explanations.explanation: Paul has just said God will reveal things to those who think differently. But his next word is "Nevertheless," and then he says to live up to what we have already attained. So the instruction is to keep walking in what you have. Stopping isn't in the verse.
Paul says, "Join one another in following my example, brothers…" (Philippians 3:17). Notice the words "Join one another…" They're meant to follow it together, not each on their own.

Peter was one of Jesus' twelve disciples (Matthew 10:2). But here Paul points to his own example, not Peter's. He says, "Join one another in following my example, brothers…" It's a fine name to guess, friend, just not the one in this verse.

Moses was the man God sent to bring His people out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10). But Paul doesn't mention him here. He says, "Join one another in following my example, brothers…" The example in this verse is Paul's own.

explanations.answer: Those who walk by the pattern he set
explanations.explanation: Paul says to carefully observe those who walk according to the pattern "…we set for you." So the examples aren't just Paul. He points past himself to anyone whose walk matches that pattern. Friend, the lesson is to watch how people walk.

explanations.answer: Those who lead the local synagogue
explanations.explanation: Paul never mentions a synagogue in this passage. He says to carefully observe those who walk according to the pattern he set for them. What counts is how they walk, not a title or a building.

explanations.answer: Those who are rich and well known
explanations.explanation: Nothing about money or fame shows up in Paul's words. He says to carefully observe those who walk according to the pattern he set for them. The thing he's watching is how people walk. A bank balance doesn't come into it.
Paul says, "Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ." That's a heavy word, and he's said it with tears. I think this one is meant to be taken seriously. Let's not rush past it.
Students is a gentle word, and it's not the one Paul uses. He says, "Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ." He says it even with tears. I think a word that heavy is worth slowing down for.

Guardians would be quite the twist, but that's not what Paul writes. He says, "Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ." That's the opposite of protecting it. And he says it with tears, and I think that tells you how much it weighs on him.

Close, but the verse says the reverse. Paul says, "Their minds are set on earthly things." So the statement is false, because heavenly things aren't what he says they're set on. Read that last line again and it's right there.
Right. Paul says the enemies of the cross have minds "…set on earthly things." He doesn't say heavenly things. Then he turns to what's different about us, and that's the next verse.

Paul says, "But our citizenship is in heaven…" The word "But" matters here. Those other folks have their minds set on earthly things, and Paul points somewhere else. Friend, heaven is the citizenship he names for us.

Paul was writing to believers in Philippi (Philippians 1:1), so I see why you picked it. But he doesn't say their citizenship is there. He says, "But our citizenship is in heaven…" That one little word covers it.
Rome never comes up in these verses. Paul says, "But our citizenship is in heaven…" You can keep your passport in the drawer on this one, friend. The citizenship he names is heaven.
Paul says we eagerly await a Savior from there, "…the Lord Jesus Christ…" He names Him plainly. No guessing needed, friend. The One we're waiting on is Jesus.
Elijah was a prophet in Israel (1 Kings 17:1). But Paul doesn't name him here. He says we eagerly await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Gabriel is an angel who stands in God's presence and brings messages (Luke 1:19). But Paul doesn't name him here. He says the Savior we eagerly await is "…the Lord Jesus Christ…" That's the name in the verse.

Paul says Jesus will transform our lowly bodies "…to be like His glorious body." Our bodies are called lowly, and His is called glorious. And the change happens by the power that enables Him to subject all things to Himself. I'd say that's quite the upgrade.

Earthly is a word Paul uses a couple of verses earlier, but he says the enemies of the cross have minds set on earthly things. Here he says Jesus will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body. So the word in this blank is glorious.
Humble is a nice word, but it's not the one Paul uses. He calls our bodies lowly, and he says they'll be like His glorious body. So the blank is about His body, and the word for it is glorious.
Paul says, "…my brothers, whom I love and long for, my joy and crown…" That's a man telling them he loves them and longs for them. I'd love to be called that by somebody, friend.
The text says otherwise. Paul writes, "…my brothers, whom I love and long for, my joy and crown…" So he does call them his joy and crown. The statement is true.
Paul says, "…that is how you must stand firm in the Lord, my beloved." He ends by calling them beloved, which fits everything he said before it. Standing firm is the last thing he asks of them here.

A visit would be nice, and I'd bake for it, friend. But Paul doesn't ask for one here. He says, "…that is how you must stand firm in the Lord, my beloved." His word to them is to stand firm, not to show up at the door.
Leaders aren't mentioned in this closing line. Paul says, "…that is how you must stand firm in the Lord, my beloved." The command is to stand firm in the Lord. A vote isn't part of it.
